newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: KLM Q1 NET SEEN DOWN AS NORTHWEST SHARE FALLS.
newsitem.headline: KLM Q1 NET SEEN DOWN AS NORTHWEST SHARE FALLS.

text.p: Dutch carrier KLM will report sharply lower first-quarter 1997/98 net profits on Tuesday but paradoxically the quality of its earnings will have significantly improved, analysts said.
The airline is expected to post first-quarter profits of 94-136 guilders, with consensus at 115 million -- less than half KLM's year-earlier figure of 271 million guilders.

In the first 1996/97 quarter, however, profits were inflated by a 245 million contribution from U.S. partner Northwest. This year, Northwest's contribution will have dwindled to around 50 million guilders, most analysts reckon.

At the level of operating profits -- considered to be a far more reliable indicator of performance -- analysts are predicting a rise of anything between 10-90 million guilders on last year's 80 million.
"The quality of earnings will be better," said Gert Jochems, chief analyst with NIB Securities. "Load factors have improved year-on-year, and fuel prices will have fallen."
"I reckon KLM's total fuel bill will have stayed more or less the same, despite an increase in activity."
ING Barings analyst Thibaud de Guerre was more cautious, saying the airline would not have escaped a higher fuel bill.
While kerosene prices had fallen, lower spot prices would take time to work through due to longer-running fuel contracts, he said.
"Total costs are still rising at too high a rate," De Guerre added. "Wage and fuel bills will be high."
But he said the airline's operating performance would be better, given its quarterly load factor -- the proportion of seats and cargo capacity filled -- was up year on year.
"Alongside a 4.6 percent-point increase in the load factor, currency exchange rates will also help lift operating profits," predicted Generale Bank's Corne Zandbergen.
A stronger dollar would boost revenues at the airline, while KLM would also likely reap some benefits from the drop in kerosene prices, he said.
